E9 Executive Track

Geopolitics & Macro

Lesson Lectures · learn

For thirty years, smart executives could mostly ignore world politics — trade flowed, borders blurred, and the cheapest factory on Earth won. That world is over. This lesson teaches you to read geopolitics like a strategist: not as scary headlines, but as a force that swings the value of your company. Tap the cards, the diagrams, and the quizzes as you go.

1 · What "geopolitics" actually means for business

Most people hear "geopolitics" and picture war. That's only a sliver. The strategist's definition is broader 👇

Geopolitics is the competing strategic priorities of nations — and the tools they use to pursue them: trade policy, industrial policy, sanctions, export controls, and yes, sometimes security and conflict. War is the loud part; tariffs and subsidies are the part that quietly reprices your supply chain.

After decades when geopolitics was benign for most global companies, there's been a trend break. Nations are competing harder, and their actions now create big, frequent "value swings" for firms. It's no longer a topic for the foreign-ministry desk — it's a board-level agenda.

"Companies now say leaders now say that this is the number one agenda that they believe could change value or create disruption for their enterprises."

— McKinsey & Company, "How business leaders can proactively navigate geopolitics" · in your corpus

2 · The vocabulary — flip to learn

These are the exact terms used by strategists at McKinsey, BCG, MIT and Eurasia Group. Tap a card to flip it.

3 · The big map: a multipolar world

For decades the world had one or two superpowers running the show. The strategist's base case for the 2030s is three pulling forces, not one. Think of it as a spectrum from "aligned with the West" to "aligned with the East," with powerful swing players in the middle. Tap each block:

"You can get stability with bi-polarity, but you can't get stability in my view with multi-polarity."

— TRIUM Global Executive MBA, "Geopolitics In Focus #1: Business leadership in the multi-polar world" · in your corpus

4 · From headlines to dollars: the value swing

Why should a CFO care about a shipping lane or a tariff vote? Because each event reprices the company. These aren't hypotheticals — they're estimates the lecturers cited from recent events:

"The US Commerce Department estimates that 1.7 plus trillion of value was lost by US companies because of those tariffs."

— McKinsey & Company, "How business leaders can proactively navigate geopolitics" · in your corpus

5 · The playbook: five moves to build the muscle

The BCG framework boils the response down to five exercises — a "corporate workout." Tap to reveal each:

Retire the single lowest-cost mega-factory. Replace it with a network of smaller factories that can flex when a pandemic, war, or tariff hits overnight.

The cheap money of the 2010s is gone. Plan investments and pricing for continued inflationary pressure from military spending, energy transition, and fragmentation.

One global HQ no longer works across rival economic systems and tech stacks. Run a set of agile regional command centers that can adapt locally.

In a world of AI and asymmetric warfare, harden at every level — systems, employees, and culture — not just the firewall.

The core move: talent, decision-making, and leadership. Hire people who sense shifts and think in scenarios, and inject a geopolitical lens into every big decision.

"To develop what I call the geopolitical muscle. No worries, I have no shares in any gym chain."

— TED, "5 Ways Leaders Can Adapt to Shifting Geopolitics | Nikolaus S. Lang" · in your corpus

6 · A worked example: the Strait of Hormuz

Watch the chain reaction the macro analysts traced live. A flare-up in the Middle East threatens the Strait of Hormuz — the chokepoint for a huge share of seaborne oil. Follow the dominoes:

① Chokepoint risk → ships fired on, a shipping lane in doubt. ② Commodity shock → crude oil spikes (Brent up ~5% in a session). ③ Inflation channel → pricier energy feeds into inflation. ④ Rates & markets → the Fed looks less likely to cut, long-dated yields hit 2026 highs, and equities fall from records.

One regional conflict, four steps, and suddenly it's on the balance sheet of a company that sells nothing in the region. That is why you can't take geopolitics out of finance.

"You cannot take geopolitics out of finance right now."

— Bloomberg Podcasts, "Business Leaders Talk Geopolitical Risk at Milken | Balance of Power" · in your corpus

⚠️ The #1 trap: confusing "decoupling" with "de-risking"

It's tempting to read every headline as the end of globalization and rip out a rival market entirely. But the data the lecturers cite shows global trade and foreign direct investment are not collapsing — and rivals like the US and China remain conflictually interdependent. The smart move is diversify and add buffers, not blindly decouple from a partner you can't actually replace.

7 · Check yourself

In the strategist's definition, which of these is NOT a normal tool of geopolitics?

Geopolitics is about the tools nations use — trade policy, industrial policy, sanctions, security. A firm's own marketing budget isn't a tool of statecraft.

Why is a multipolar world considered more uncertain than a bipolar one?

More poles = more independent actors (including swing middle powers), so outcomes are harder to predict. The lecturer was explicit that it means more uncertainty, not an inevitable war.

A flare-up near the Strait of Hormuz spikes oil prices. What's the most likely knock-on effect the analysts described?

Pricier energy feeds inflation, which makes the Fed less likely to cut rates — rippling into bond yields and equities far beyond the region.

🔎 One subtlety → your bridge to the next course

Notice how a geopolitical shock travels: chokepoint → oil → inflation → interest rates → asset prices. Those last two links are the heart of macroeconomics — how central banks set rates and why the "cheap money" era ended. A practitioner thread in your corpus (the reported "Core 5 / C5" national-security strategy floating US, China, Russia, India, Japan as co-managers of global order) shows the multipolar map being drawn in real time. Next we connect the political map to the macro machine that prices it.

🎯 Your move

Pick one company you know well. Write its one-page geopolitical exposure map: (1) name its top 1–2 supply-chain chokepoints, (2) name the single country it can least afford to lose, and (3) pick one of the five BCG moves to start with. You've just done the first rep of building the geopolitical muscle.

So what's the most favorite scenario all over the world, from southern Chile to northern Japan? It's a scenario which we call "back to the future." Then there is a second bloc, which I describe as the new Eastern Bloc. And that's actually China and Russia growing together with countries such as North Korea and Iran joining this bloc. And then there’s a third bloc. And I don’t call it bloc. I don’t want to call it bloc, because I think it's more of a grouping of countries, where we have a series of middle powers, regional powers such as India, Indonesia, the GCC countries, that are playing a role of staying in balance between those two blocs.

These countries have huge assets, be it natural resources, abundant talent, interesting geographical position. And they leverage these assets to develop a non-aligned path between the two other blocs. And they develop spheres of influence across Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America. So we are in this multipolar world. What does this mean for companies and corporate leaders? Companies and corporate leaders need to navigate and they need to develop a geopolitical muscle. The new reality is you need to have a network of small factories all over the world. You need to have flexible supply chains that are able to respond to external shocks. Exercise two. Prepare for continued inflation and price volatility. I know no one wants to hear it, but I think the current discussion of price cuts is interesting. But the reality is that the cheap money of the 2010s is gone. Much more real is a continuous inflationary pressure we will see through geopolitical shifts, increased military spending and the cost of energy transition.

So companies need to prepare in their investment and pricing decisions how to handle this continued inflationary pressure and pricing volatility. Third, design your organization for a fragmented world. The time where you were handling a company and a multinational company from one headquarter, is gone. In a world, in a multipolar world, where you have different economic systems, political ideologies and technical stacks, you will need to set up your company as a collection of regional command centers that are agile and independent and can perfectly adapt to the new realities. Fourth, prepare for cybersecurity.

In a multipolar world where AI and asymmetric warfare are likely to become the new normal, companies need to prepare for cyber attacks, both on a system level, but also on an employee level and a culture level. Fifth, and this is the core of it, develop the geopolitical muscle. So what is it? It's about talent. It's about decision making. And it's about leadership. Talent. Companies need to hire and develop talent that is able to sense geopolitical shifts, that is able to think in scenarios, that is able to redesign supply chains, that is able to define new strategies. Second, decision making.

While investment decisions and project decisions and strategies need, of course, to consider dimensions in finance, in legal and HR, it is critical to inject a geopolitical perspective in the way how you make decisions. And last on leadership, let me dream a little bit. I still think that managers continue to be good managers. But I would hope that their decision is also influenced by the way how historians, economists and politicians decide and think, in order to pivot their strategies to the new realities. So let me conclude this wake up call with a simple alternative. Either you continue with your geopolitical napping, (Laughter) or you build your geopolitical muscle.
